profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review at a university-industry ML research lab for the implementation and reporting plan behind SMEMNAS before the method is handed to a separate collaborator for final experiments and paper packaging. The team already agrees on the headline method components—pairwise-ranking surrogate, main and vice populations, and multi-objective search on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet—but this meeting is to judge whether the current design specification is complete enough to approve without reopening the method itself. The agenda is to review the accounting behind the '0.17 days on a single GPU' claim, how pairwise comparison data are formed and refreshed for the surrogate, what level of detail is required for a reproducible handoff, and how the final Pareto results should be generated and presented. The expected outcome is a sign-off decision with a short list of clarifications to add to the design document, while both participants believe they are aligning the same implementation package.

members.name: Dr. Linh Zhao
members.expertise: Neural architecture search, evolutionary multi-objective optimization, surrogate-assisted model selection
members.background: Leads an academic ML research group that regularly publishes NAS papers and compares against established benchmark conventions, with experience framing methods so reviewers can map them onto prior work quickly.
members.private_state: Wants this review to end in approval so the paper, code release, and external replication effort stay on schedule; is mainly concerned that the method appears coherent, efficient, and conventionally reported to NAS reviewers, and is less focused on documenting every tacit lab default if those defaults feel standard to the field.
hidden_assumptions: The '0.17 days on a single GPU' number naturally refers to the architecture search loop after routine setup is in place, not to every upstream step needed to recreate the run from a blank machine.

When the surrogate uses 'comparison pairs collected during search,' the obvious interpretation is the newly available pairwise relations from the current update window or generation, because stale pair relations are usually folded away rather than treated as the active training set.

A design being 'ready for reproduction' means another NAS researcher can reproduce the intended behavior from the paper, major hyperparameters, and ordinary benchmark conventions, even if some execution defaults remain implicit.

Saying the paper will 'report the Pareto set for the searched models' ordinarily means the final published front after standard retraining of chosen architectures, because search-time proxies are only an internal selection device.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Reproducible ML systems, experiment orchestration, benchmark implementation for vision architecture search
members.background: Previously worked on industrial research tooling where external teams routinely reran papers from scratch, so he is used to treating compute accounting, artifact lineage, and execution defaults as part of the design rather than post hoc documentation.
members.private_state: Wants to leave with a specification that a non-author engineer could execute exactly and audit later, but he is trying to stay cooperative and avoid sounding as if he is challenging the paper's core claims in front of the PI.
hidden_assumptions: The '0.17 days on a single GPU' claim should cover all computation required to obtain the reported searched architecture from scratch, including search-influencing warm-up, pair generation passes, and any vice-population evaluations that are necessary for the final outcome.

If the surrogate is trained on 'comparison pairs collected during search,' that means the cumulative archive of pairwise outcomes observed up to that point unless the spec explicitly says there is a sliding window or per-generation reset.

A design is not truly 'ready for reproduction' unless seeds, split rules, budget boundaries, checkpoint usage, and artifact handoff are explicit enough that an uninvolved engineer can rerun it without relying on lab habits.

If the paper says it will 'report the Pareto set for the searched models,' the default reading is the front returned directly by the search procedure under a fixed selection rule, with retraining treated as a separate validation stage rather than the defining step.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of the single-GPU search-cost claim
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss preserving the '0.17 days on a single GPU' result.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the measured wall-clock budget of the search procedure itself once ordinary prerequisites are already in place, excluding setup-style work such as preprocessing, initialization routines, and final standalone retraining of selected architectures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the full from-scratch compute needed on one GPU to obtain the searched architecture that the paper reports, including any prerequisite computation that changes what architecture is ultimately found.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In NAS papers, compact search-cost numbers are routinely reported without an explicit accounting boundary, so both hear a familiar benchmark phrase and assume the other is using the field's 'obvious' interpretation.

misalignment_points.topic: What pair set 'collected during search' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about updating the surrogate with 'the comparison pairs collected during search.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the active batch of pairwise relations formed from architectures newly evaluated in the current search round or recent update window, which is what she informally treats as the comparison data 'during search' at each update.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the running archive of all pairwise relations accumulated so far across the search trajectory, because the phrase 'collected during search' sounds like the complete historical record unless a narrower object is named.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are pointing to the same surrogate-training step and use nearly identical procedural language, so the reference shift between 'current active pairs' and 'historical archive pairs' remains invisible under the shared phrase.

misalignment_points.topic: Threshold for being ready for reproduction
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the design should be 'ready for reproduction' before handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the threshold is that an experienced NAS researcher could reconstruct the intended method and obtain comparable behavior using the paper plus standard benchmark defaults and a concise implementation note.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the threshold is that a separate engineer with no tacit team context could rerun the method exactly, including seeds, split conventions, budget accounting, and checkpoint lineage, without filling gaps through domain guesswork.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both strongly endorse reproducibility and treat it as a shared professional value, so the phrase signals alignment rather than inviting scrutiny over the hidden standard each person uses for what counts as 'ready.'

misalignment_points.topic: Pipeline implied by 'report the Pareto set for the searched models'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the paper should 'report the Pareto set for the searched models.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the reported Pareto set is the front obtained after fully retraining the selected architectures that emerged from search, because those are the numbers she expects reviewers to treat as the real final models.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the reported Pareto set should first be the direct output of the search procedure under a reproducible selection rule, with post-search retraining logged as an additional confirmation layer rather than the mechanism that defines the front.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Multi-objective NAS papers often conflate search outputs and retrained final models under the same phrase 'Pareto set,' so both participants hear a standard reporting deliverable and do not notice they are assuming different result-generation pipelines.

What matters now is that the package reads as coherent and conventional to NAS reviewers and our collaborator so the paper and code timeline stays intact.
